title: Centripetal acceleration: the sideways grip a car needs on a curve
examples: Why do cars skid on sharp bends?
What provides the centripetal force for a car turning?

forces.label: Tyre grip 9.6 kN
forces.ask: What provides the centripetal force for a car turning?

explain.say: Drive round a roundabout and you feel pushed to the outside. In fact, nothing pushes you out: your body wants to go straight, and the car pulls you inwards. Anything moving in a circle accelerates towards the centre, even at steady speed, because its direction keeps changing. Look at the car from behind.

draw.text: Centripetal acceleration: the sideways grip a car needs on a curve

forces.label: Tyre grip 9.6 kN
forces.ask: What provides the centripetal force for a car turning?

draw.text: Car 1200 kg at 20 m/s on a curve of radius 50 m

explain.say: That inward acceleration is called centripetal acceleration. It equals v squared over r. At 20 metres per second on a curve of radius 50 metres, that is 400 over 50, which is 8 metres per second squared. Where does the inward force come from? See the sideways arrow at the tyres?

forces.label: Tyre grip 9.6 kN
forces.ask: What provides the centripetal force for a car turning?

explain.say: It is friction between the tyres and the road! The force needed is m times a: 1200 times 8, which is 9600 newtons, pointing to the centre of the curve. Friction can give at most mu times the weight, so mu must be at least 8 over 9.81, about 0.82. Is that easy on a wet road?

forces.label: Tyre grip 9.6 kN
forces.ask: What provides the centripetal force for a car turning?

explain.say: No, wet roads may only give about 0.5, so the car would skid outwards. Look at the graph: acceleration grows with speed squared. At 15 metres per second it drops to 4.5. And on the gentler 100 metre curve, everything halves. Which matters more, slowing down or a wider curve?

curves.label: Radius 50 m
curves.ask: Why does the needed acceleration grow so fast with speed?

explain.say: Slowing down, because speed is squared! Great work. Real link: highways and racing tracks bank their curves so part of the road reaction points inwards and helps the tyres. Exam tip: centripetal force is never a new force on your diagram; it is the job done by friction, tension or a reaction. Challenge: what speed needs only mu equals 0.5 here?

draw.text: Centripetal force is a role, not an extra force

faq.a: It is the acceleration of a body moving in a circle, pointing towards the centre. Its size is v squared over r, or omega squared times r.

faq.q: What provides the centripetal force for a car turning?
faq.a: Sideways friction between the tyres and the road. On a banked curve, part of the normal reaction helps too.
asks: what force keeps a car on a curve

faq.q: Why does the needed acceleration grow so fast with speed?
faq.a: Centripetal acceleration is v squared over r, so doubling the speed needs four times the acceleration and four times the grip.

faq.q: Why do cars skid on sharp bends?
faq.a: If the needed inward force, m v squared over r, is larger than the maximum friction the tyres can give, the car slides outwards along a wider path.
asks: why do cars slide on corners

faq.a: In the ground frame, no: there is only the inward centripetal force, and your body tends to go straight. In a rotating frame it appears as an apparent outward force.

facts: A body moving in a circle at constant speed has an acceleration of v squared over r towards the centre.
On a flat curve, the highest safe speed is the square root of mu times g times r.

quiz.show: Same curve, three times the speed: the sideways grip needed becomes…
